activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Weston ran to the play kitchen at daycare. He wanted his apple for snack time. But there were lots of apples there. Some were toys. One was real.

Miss Ana said, "Snack time soon, Weston." Weston picked up a red apple. He squeezed it. It was hard and light. He put it down. He picked up another one. This one was heavy. He held it close to his nose. It smelled sweet. The toy apples had no smell at all.

"You found the real one," said Miss Ana. "The hard ones are toys. Toys are for pretend food. The heavy one is real. Real food smells good."

Weston smiled. He took his real apple to the little table. It was sticky from his friend's honey at breakfast, so Miss Ana washed it with warm water.

Then Weston took a big bite. "Crunch!" he said. Miss Ana laughed and sat down next to him.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Violet ran to the swings. Her dad sat on the bench nearby. But the big swing was taken. A boy was on it.

Violet wanted that swing. She grabbed the chain. The boy yelled, "Hey!" Violet stepped back. Her shoes felt itchy and she wiggled her toes.

"Say sorry," said the boy's grandma. Violet looked down. "Sorry," she said quietly. The boy said, "It's okay." Then his grandma helped him off the swing.

The swing was free now. Violet climbed on. "Dad, please push me!" she called. Dad came and pushed. Up went Violet, high like a bird.

"Thank you, Dad!" she shouted. Dad laughed. "You said the magic word," he said. Violet kicked her feet. "Please gets pushes!" she said. Dad pushed her again, and the swing went zip through the air.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Sienna was going on a big trip. She rode the train with Mama and Papa. The train went chug, chug, chug. Sienna counted what she saw out the window. "One cow. Two trees. Three little houses."

Then Sienna reached for her bunny. Her bunny was her best friend. He was not in her arms. He was not in her lap. Sienna looked and looked. "Where is Bunny?"

Sienna thought hard. She remembered her bed. She remembered her warm blanket. "I left Bunny on my bed," she said. "That is why he is not here. He is not here because I left him at home." A big tear rolled down her cheek. Mama gave her a soft hug.

Papa opened the window a tiny bit. Fresh air came in. It smelled like grass and rain. Sienna held her little chocolate egg. She held it too long in her warm hand. The chocolate began to melt. Sticky, drippy chocolate! Mama laughed and wiped her fingers with a napkin.

Then came a small surprise. Sienna opened her small pink backpack for a fresh tissue. Something soft was inside. It was Bunny! Mama had tucked him in at the door. "You packed me, Mama!" Sienna said. She hugged Bunny tight all the way to Grandma's house.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. On the table was a library book. It had a bear on the cover. It was Aaron's favorite book.

Aaron opened the book. The pages had little marks on them. Grandma pointed at the marks. "Those marks are words," she said. "Words tell the story." Grandma held the book. She turned the pages one by one. She started at the front. She read to the back. Aaron listened to every page.

"I want to keep this book forever," Aaron said. Grandma shook her head. "The library lets us borrow it," she said. "We take it home, but we bring it back by Friday. Other people want to read it too." Aaron felt sad. He held the book tight. "What if someone else takes my bear book?" he asked. Grandma sat close to him. "We can borrow it again," she said. "The library will not say no."

So they read the book one more time. Then it was Friday. "We must hurry," said Grandma. "School is over and the library closes soon." They drove to the library together. Aaron put the book in the return box all by himself. He saw a girl pick it up right away. She hugged it and smiled.

"Grandma, the girl has my book because I gave it back," Aaron said. Grandma took his hand. "And next week, it can be yours again." Aaron smiled big. "Words tell the story," he said. "And books go front to back." Grandma laughed and hugged him. "Let's pick a new one to take home," she said.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Willow sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "What will happen there?" she asked. "The dentist will look at your teeth," said Mom. "She has a little mirror. It lifts up high, so she can see the top teeth."

Willow held her toy cat. "The mirror will not fit in my mouth," she said. "My mouth is small." Mom smiled. "Open your mouth wide. Then it fits."

At the dentist, a kind lady said, "Open wide." Willow opened her mouth wide. The little mirror went in. "I can see your teeth," said the dentist. Willow did not fall off the chair. She sat very still.

"My mouth was small," said Willow. "Then I made it big. The mirror went in because I opened wide." Mom hugged her. "That was smart thinking," said Mom. The dentist gave Willow a sticker. Willow held it up all the way home.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Joshua sat at the craft table at summer camp. He wore his big yellow hat. The sun was high in the sky outside. Today he was making a paper sun with long yellow rays.

Joshua put glue on a ray. He stuck it on right away. Then he held the paper up. The ray slid down and fell off. "Oh no," said Joshua. His friend Mia looked over. "My ray fell too," she said.

Joshua touched the glue. It was wet and sticky. He pressed the ray on again. This time he counted slowly. One, two, three. He kept his hands still. He watched the glue. It began to dry. He let go. The ray stayed!

"The glue was wet," Joshua said. "Wet glue slides. Dry glue sticks."

Outside, the campers began to sing. Joshua sang too. He held his paper sun up high, and all the rays stayed on.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Gabriella went to Mia's house. Mia had a big blue blanket on the floor. "This is the sea," said Mia. "My doll will swim in it." The doll jumped in and slid under the blanket.

Gabriella wanted her bear to swim too. But her bear was scared. He sat on the edge and did not move. "He needs a boat," said Gabriella. She found a shoebox. Now the bear had a boat. He sailed right across the blue blanket sea.

Then Mia's doll got cold. "Her skin is cold from the water," said Gabriella. She wrapped the doll in a sock. The doll got warm and cozy. A spotted cat puppet came to check on them. He was the sea doctor.

Mia yawned. "The sea is sleepy now," she said. The blanket waves went flat and still. "Night night, sea," said Gabriella. She patted the blanket three times.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Asher went to the store with Mama. In his bag was a library book about soft kittens. "Mine," said Asher. "I will keep it forever."

At the store, Asher saw signs. One sign said MILK. "Mama, that word says milk!" "Yes," said Mama. "Words tell us things." The book had words too. Asher turned the pages, one, two, three, four. The story went from the front to the back. He read it that way, front to back.

But Asher had a plan. He would hide the book under his coat. Then the library could not take it back. He tucked it in. He zipped up. Then he heard a small sound. "Meow," said the book. Asher laughed. "Silly book, you cannot meow!"

Mama smiled. "We take the book back on library day," she said. "Other kids read it too." So Asher gave the book a hug. He held it soft and close. "One more read," he said. "Front to back. Then you go home to your friends."

At bedtime, Asher turned the pages. One, two, three. The soft kitten found her mama at the end. "Good for you," said Asher. He patted the cover and said, "Library day is soon. But you are my friend first."

The book went into the bag all by itself, and Asher waved. "Bye bye, little meow."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor skip, skip, skipped to the door to meet her. Grandma had a big suitcase and a tiny pillow in her bag.

On Monday, Grandma fell asleep in the middle of the day. She slept in the chair by the swing. "Grandma, why are you sleepy?" Eleanor asked. "It is not even night!"

Grandma yawned. "I flew on a plane for a long, long time," she said. Eleanor wondered about that. Did the plane make Grandma tired?

On Tuesday, Grandma napped again. On Wednesday, she napped just a little bit. By Friday, Grandma was awake all day. Eleanor clapped her hands. "Grandma, you are fixed!" Grandma laughed and picked her up for a big hug.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Cooper sat at the little blue table. He was making a sun with yellow paper. He picked up the glue bottle. He squeezed and squeezed. Glue went everywhere. His paper got very wet. The soft yellow paper tore a little bit. Cooper made a sad face.

His teacher brought a small glass of water for his hands. Cooper dipped his fingers in. The room was noisy with kids cutting and pasting. Then Cooper got a new piece of paper. This time he made one small dot of glue. He pressed on a yellow circle. It stayed on. It did not tear. Cooper pushed it again. It still stayed.

"The big glue made the paper tear," Cooper said. "Little glue makes it stay." He held up his sun. It shined all yellow and whole. "Look, teacher! I fixed it with a tiny dot!"

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Raphael stood by the big window at the community centre. Snack time was coming. Two bowls of crackers sat on the table. Miss Maya said, "Can you tell me which bowl has more?"

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Then he counted the second bowl from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He frowned. Did counting from the other end change things? He counted the first bowl again, starting from the other side. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Still seven!

"Miss Maya, I got seven both times," he said. "It is seven, whichever cracker I count first." Miss Maya smiled and gave the bigger bowl to the twins. They were extra hungry today.

One cracker was broken in half. Raphael ate it first. Then his ice pop began to melt in the sun, so he drank it from the bowl like juice.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Nolan woke up from his sleep at Grandma's house. Today was a big day. He was getting his very first haircut!

Grandma held his hand. They walked to the salon down the street. They passed the playground on the way. "I can play after," said Nolan.

The hairdresser had a shiny spray bottle. She squirted water on Nolan's hair. Squirt, squirt! His hair was wet now. The wet hair stuck together in little points. The scissors went snip, snip. The wet pieces fell down like tiny dark rain. They stuck to the cape and made it not clean.

Nolan watched in the mirror. He touched his dry hair at home sometimes. Dry hair puffed up and flew away. Wet hair stayed on the cape in little lines.

"Look," said Nolan. "The water makes my hair stick. That is why it falls down!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "Wet hair is easy to cut."

Soon the haircut was done. Nolan jumped off the chair. "Playground time!" he said.

Grandma laughed. They ran out the door, hand in hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Eliana sat on the rug in the living room. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Aunt Jo sat on the couch with a bowl of popcorn. The big game was on TV. Everyone wore blue shirts.

Then Eliana saw a bright spot on the screen. The sun was on the TV. She could not see the ball. The bright spot hid it. "I can't see," said Grandpa. He leaned to one side. Aunt Jo leaned too.

Eliana looked at the window. The sun came from there. She stood up. She took the curtain in her little hands. She pulled it across. The curtain slid shut. Now the window was closed. The bright spot went away. The screen was clear and dark. "There is no sun now," said Eliana. "The sun made the spot." Grandpa clapped. On the TV, a player kicked the ball into the net. The crowd went loud. Everyone jumped up. Eliana hugged the popcorn bowl. "We did it," she said.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Kai sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But where was the green paint? He looked in the cup. He looked in the box. No green. "That's bad," said Kai.

His teacher Miss Ana said, "What colors do you see?" Kai looked hard. "Red. Blue. Yellow." He touched the yellow cup. It felt cool and slippery. He touched the blue cup too.

Then Kai had an idea. What if yellow and blue mixed together? He zipped his brush into the yellow paint. He zipped it again into the blue paint. Swish, swish, round and round on the paper. The paint made a new color. It was green!

"Look, look!" said Kai. "Yellow and blue make green! That is why there was no green cup." He painted a fat green frog with big eyes. Outside, the summer sun came in the window. It warmed his hand. "Miss Ana," he asked, "what does red and yellow make?"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. The soup was warm. Grandma began to pour the milk.

Then everyone stopped. Nobody ate. Emile looked around. Why was the food just sitting there?

"Hold my hand," said Grandma. Emile held her hand. Cousin Lou held his other hand. Everyone at the table made one big circle with their hands.

Then everyone said the blessing together. "Thank you for our food." Emile did not know the words yet. He opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His cheeks went pink.

"Just hum," said Lou with a grin. "Nobody can tell."

So Emile hummed. He hummed very loud. He sounded like a little bee.

Grandma laughed. "Now we eat!" she said. Because the blessing was done, everyone picked up a spoon at last.

After lunch, Emile found Grandma's big sun hat. He put it on. "Thank you for our food," he said to the hat.

"That's it!" said Grandma. "Say it two more times before dinner. Then it will stick like glue."

Emile said it to the hat. He said it to the cat. The cat walked away.

At dinner, everyone held hands again. This time Emile knew just what to do. He held on tight and said, "Thank you for our food."

Lou clapped. Grandma kissed his head. Then everyone picked up a spoon at the very same time.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Sienna ran to the table. Lunch was ready! Her hands were dirty from the sandbox.

"Hands first," said Mama. "Wash with soap."

Sienna looked at her hands. Sand was on them. Yucky germs were on them too. Germs were too far away to see, but they were there.

She pushed the bench to the sink. She turned on the water. She pumped the soap. Bubbles! Big white bubbles!

"Now we count," said Mama. "Count to twenty."

"One, two, three," said Sienna. She rubbed and rubbed. "Four, five, six."

"Sing the happy song," said Mama.

Sienna sang. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" The bubbles grew and grew. "Eleven, twelve!"

She washed the backs of her hands. She washed between her fingers. "Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!"

Rinse, rinse. The bubbles ran down. "Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!"

Mama gave her the towel. Sienna looked at her hands. Clean! Pink and shiny clean!

Sienna lifted her sandwich up high. She took a big bite.

"Mama!" she said. "Soap makes germs go away. That is why we wash!"

Then she looked at the towel. A tiny ladybug sat on it!

"Hello, ladybug," said Sienna. "Did you wash your hands too?"

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Asher sat in the big chair. It was his first haircut! The barber put a cape on him. The cape went snap, snap, snap.

The barber cut with his scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. "Look, look!" said Asher. The hairs landed on the cape. They did not fall on his shirt.

The cape caught them! The hairs sat on the cape because it was big and wide.

"Now you get a sticker," said the barber. He put it in Asher's hand. Asher held it tight so he would not miss it.

Asher jumped down from the big chair. "I got a haircut!" he said. "My hairs fell on my cape!" He ran to show his mom the sticker.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Beatrice ran to the block corner at school. She saw the big red robot toy. Tom was holding it. Beatrice wanted it too.

"Give it!" said Beatrice. She pulled the robot. Tom pulled back. The robot fell on the floor. It made a loud crash. Now nobody had the robot.

Miss Kay knelt down. "We take turns," she said. "Tom, you play first. Then Beatrice." Tom set a timer on the shelf. When it rang, it was Beatrice's turn.

Beatrice held the robot. Tom waited, but his lip looked sad. Beatrice looked at him. "You can push the button," she said. Tom pushed the button. The robot blinked. "Nice robot!" said Tom. Beatrice waved the robot's arm. "Beep beep!" she said.

Then the timer rang again. Tom got his turn. Beatrice waited. The timer made turns fair. Nobody had to pull. Nobody had to cry.

"Your turn, my turn," said Beatrice. "That is how it works." Tom smiled and pushed the button again.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brielle sat in her reading nook. She wanted to spell her name. But the letters looked like squiggly lines to her. She felt mad. She threw her sock on the floor.

Mama sat down next to her. She pointed to the first letter. "This is B," Mama said. "It says buh. Listen. Buh, buh, Brielle."

Brielle tapped the letter. "Buh," she said. Then she looked at her book. "Buh, bear!" The bear on the page started with B too.

She looked at the sock on the floor. "Suh, sock!" she said. S made the suh sound. She laughed and picked it up.

Brielle traced B with her finger. Slow, then fast. Then she said, "B-R-I-E-L-L-E. That is me!"

She hugged her book tight and read the letters again, all by herself.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kayden wanted his red plane. It was not in the toy box. "Where is it?" he asked. Mom sat next to him. "Think about yesterday," she said. Kayden thought. Yesterday he flew the plane in the yard. He left it by the big tree. "I remember now!" he said.

They went outside together. The plane was wet. Yesterday the rain came after Kayden went inside. The rain made the plane wet. "The rain fell on it," said Kayden. "That is why it is wet." Mom smiled and nodded.

Kayden began to cry a little. "Is my plane broken?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "We will dry it now. Later it will be dry and shiny." They wiped the plane with a soft towel. They put it by the sunny window.

"Now we wait," said Mom. "Tomorrow it will be all dry." Kayden held the plane up to the light. "Fly tomorrow," he told it. Mom laughed and kissed his head.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Elizabeth lived on a farm with her grandpa. Today Grandpa had a game. "Can you find your five senses?" he asked.

Elizabeth held up one finger. "Eyes see!" she said. She saw a black cow in the field. Two fingers. "Ears hear!" The cow said moo. That was three? No, two. She laughed at herself.

Three fingers. "Nose smells!" She sniffed the cow. "Phew!" said Grandpa, and they both giggled.

Four fingers. "Tongue tastes!" Grandpa gave her a sweet red apple from a basket.

One finger was left. Elizabeth looked at it. What did hands do? She patted the cow. The cow was soft and warm. "Hands feel!" she shouted. "The cow feels soft because I touch it!"

"Five senses, five fingers," said Grandpa. "Now let's go bathe that smelly cow."

The cow ran the other way. "Moo!" said the cow.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Sadie sat on a small log at summer camp. It was time for lunch. The counselor said, "Wash your hands first."

Sadie ran to the water pump. She got her hands wet. She rubbed on soap. Then she rinsed fast and ran back.

"Too fast," said the counselor. "Germs need twenty seconds with soap."

Sadie did not know what twenty seconds was. The counselor said, "Sing the happy birthday song twice. That is twenty seconds."

At snack time, Sadie tried it. She got her hands wet. She put on soap. She sang the song one time. She kept rubbing. She sang it again. Bubbles sat on her fingers like small clouds.

After the toilet, Sadie sang too. She counted the songs, not just splashes.

Later, Sadie looked at her clean hands. "The song makes the germs sleep," she said, and took a big bite of her apple.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Ryan was at summer camp. Lunch was coming. His tummy felt hungry for sandwiches.

A man named Sam stood by a big sink. "Come wash your hands," Sam said. Ryan ran over. He got soap on his hands. He rinsed it off fast. Then he grabbed a sandwich.

Then Ryan looked at his hands. He saw dirt on them still. He put the sandwich down. "Yuck," he said. "My hands still have dirt."

"Try again," said Sam. "Count with me." Sam rubbed his hands with soap. He counted to twenty. "One, two, three..." Ryan rubbed his hands too. The soap got bubbly. They counted all the way to twenty.

Ryan rinsed the bubbles off. He looked close. The dirt was gone! "The soap needed more time," Ryan said.

A girl named Mia could not reach the soap. Ryan got a small stool for her. "Thank you," said Mia. "That was polite," said Sam.

Then Ryan sat down and ate his sandwich. It tasted good. After lunch he had to use the toilet. When he came out, he went right back to the sink. He counted to twenty again.

"Twenty seconds," said Ryan, holding up his clean hands. "Now I can play."

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. It was yellow and shiny. It smelled like fresh wood.

"I will write my name!" said Lucas. He grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The line came out fat and wobbly. It did not look like a letter at all. "Oh no," said Lucas. "My L looks like a worm."

Mama sat down next to him. She picked up her own pencil. She held it with just three fingers, pinched near the tip, like a little crab claw. Lucas watched. He tried it too. Pinch, pinch. He made a skinny little line down. Then a little line across. "One, two, an L!" shouted Lucas.

"Now the U," said Mama. Lucas drew one big curve. "U!" he said. Then C, then A, then S. "L, U, C, A, S," he counted out loud. He looked at the paper. There it was. His name. Five letters, all in a row. "I pinch, and the letters come out beautiful!" said Lucas.

"You wrote your own name," said Mama. "We will hang it up for everyone to see. Daddy will read it after he comes home." Lucas clapped his hands. "My letters live on the paper now!" he said. He tapped the L one more time. "Hello, L."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Bennett went to the park with a cold popsicle. It was a hot day. The sun made everything warm.

Bennett saw a big tree. It made a big shadow. He also saw a small flower. It made a small shadow. Bennett held his popsicle up to the sun. Drip, drip! The red juice ran down his hand. "Oh no," said Bennett. "The sun is hot. My popsicle is melting fast."

Bennett ran slow, then fast. He stood in the big shadow under the tree. The shadow was cool. His popsicle stayed cold. "Look, Mom! The shadow helps!" He licked it with a straight, happy face. A little child ran by and pointed. A squirrel sat in the tree, holding a nut like a tiny popsicle. Bennett waved at it. "Hi, squirrel! This is my shady spot."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Addison sat on the bottom step at Grandma's house. She wanted the big red ball. Cousin Max had the big red ball. He bounced it high. Addison watched. Her bottom stayed on the step.

Grandma came out with two cups of juice. "One for Max," she said. "One for Addison. We take turns with the ball too." Max stopped bouncing. He rolled the ball to Addison. Addison hugged it. Then she rolled it back. Max laughed. They sent the ball back and forth. It went to Max, then to Addison, then to Max again.

Grandma put cookies on a plate. "Share them," she said. Addison took one cookie. She gave the plate to Max. Max took one cookie too. The cookies were tasty. Addison said, "When we take turns, we both get to play." Then she rolled the ball one more time. Max caught it.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Josephine was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Josephine wanted to draw on it, but she did not know how to start it. "What if I break it?" she asked.

Mia's mom smiled. "You will not break it," she said. "Just try."

Josephine put one finger on the round button. She held it and counted. One, two, three. The screen lit up! "The button makes it turn on," Josephine said. "I held it, so it woke up."

Next, Mia showed her the little paint picture. Josephine tapped it with her finger. The drawing app opened. She picked a thin brush and drew a big yellow sun. She drew a red cat, too. "My cat!" she said. "I win, I made a cat!"

Then it was time for a snack. "Do I just leave it here?" Josephine asked. "No," said Mia. "We put it away." Josephine tapped the button once, quick and light. The screen went to sleep. She set the tablet on the shelf, safe and flat.

"You did it all by yourself," said Mia's mom. Josephine sat down at the table. She took a warm cookie in her hand. The tablet rested quietly on the shelf, waiting for the next picture.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Weston ran to the big tree in the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. It was not in the toy box. Where could it be? A noisy crow sat in the tree. "Caw, caw!" it called.

Weston looked under the green grass. No ball. He looked by the blue water bowl. No ball. Then he saw something in the tree. Was it a red apple? No. It was his ball! The crow had put it on a branch. Why? The crow liked bright red things. "The crow took my red ball because it is red," Weston said.

Weston put his yellow truck on the grass. The crow flew down. It picked up the yellow truck! Weston laughed and grabbed his red ball. He hugged it tight. "Thank you, noisy bird!" he called.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sophie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. She reached with her fork. She reached with her hand. The basket was too far.

Daddy was cutting carrots now. He said, "I will pass the bread later, when I sit down."

Sophie waited. She watched the carrots go round and round. She looked at the flower in the jar. It was the last flower from yesterday. It had been closed this morning. Now it was open wide.

Sophie looked again at the basket. Daddy sat down. He passed her the bread.

"I waited and now I have it," Sophie said. She took a big bite. "Tomorrow can we have bread again?"

"Yes," said Daddy. "First we eat today's bread."

Sophie smiled and reached for the butter.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Jackson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil and paper. He wanted to write his name.

He held the pencil in his fist. He made a mark. It was a big blob. "Oh no," said Jackson. "I miss the lines."

Mom sat down next to him. She picked up her own pencil. She held it with her fingers, near the tip. Jackson watched. He tried it too. He pinched the pencil like Mom.

"Now my hand can see where to go," said Jackson. The pencil made a nice straight line. He drew a big J. Then a small a. The J looked pointy, like a hook on a door.

Jackson wrote more letters. He missed the c and made it look like a wet worm. He laughed and tried again. This time the c curled just right.

"Look, Mom! Jackson!" he said. His name sat on the paper. Mom clapped her hands. Jackson drew one more J, just for fun.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay at Sienna's house. "How long?" Sienna asked. "Seven sleeps," said Grandma. Sienna counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven sleeps was a whole week!

Grandma would sleep on a big air bed in Sienna's room. They pumped it up together. Then they read a story. Then they slept.

In the morning, the bed was flat! Grandma was on the floor. "Oh no," said Grandma. Sienna looked all around the bed. She found the little plug. It was not pushed in! "The plug came out," said Sienna. "That is why the bed went flat." They pushed the plug in tight. They pumped the bed up again. It stayed big and bouncy all night. Sienna jumped on it once, just to check. "Seven sleeps," she said, "and a bouncy bed too!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Arlo ran to the big slide. But the slide was snowy. The snow was soft and white. Arlo touched it with his mittens. It was cold.

"Mom, the slide is all snowy," said Arlo. Mom sat on the bench. "The sun is out now," she said. "Let us wait and watch."

Arlo waited. He grabbed a stick and drew in the snow. He made a circle. He made a line. Then he looked up. The sun was warm on his face. The white snow on the slide was getting small. It dripped, drip, drip, down the legs.

"The sun makes the snow melt," said Arlo. "The snow is little now." He put his hand on the slide. It was just a bit wet. He waited some more. At last the slide was clear. Arlo climbed up, whoosh, down he went! He went down three more times.

On the walk home, Mom said, "Yesterday the snow came. Today the sun melted it." Arlo smiled. "Tomorrow at school I will draw the slide at my desk," he said. "I will draw the drip, drip, drip."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Matteo went to the temple with his Papa. It was a special day. After the songs, everyone sat down for bread and soup at long tables.

Papa held out his hand. "We say the blessing first," he said. Matteo took Papa's hand. He took Nana's hand too. Everyone at the table held hands. Then they all said the words together. "Thank you for our food. Amen."

Matteo did not know the words yet. So he just listened. Then he saw the bread. It looked warm and good. He reached for it with his free hand. His elbow bumped his cup. Water splashed onto the cloth.

Nana helped him wipe it up. "Wait for the Amen," she said softly. "Then we eat."

Matteo waited. He held hands. He listened to the words. One, two, three, then "Amen." Now everyone picked up bread at the same time. Matteo took a big bite. It was warm and good.

After the meal, Matteo drew with a crayon. He drew the long table and all the hands. "Amen means go," he told Papa. "When we say it, we eat." Papa smiled. "You are a lucky boy," he said. "You learned our blessing today." Matteo put his crayon down and said, "Amen."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Maverick went to the garden with his grandma. He had four little seeds in his hand. One seed, two seeds, three seeds, four. He made a hole and dropped them in. He patted the soft dirt down.

The sun was hot that day. Maverick slipped off his shoe and sat on a piece of wood to rest. He looked at his dirt. "Where are my plants?" he asked. Every day he came back. Every day he saw only dirt.

Then one morning, four little green leaves popped up. But by noon, they were droopy and sad. Maverick touched the dirt. It was dry. He ran to the tap and filled his small can. He poured the water on the leaves. The next day, the leaves stood up tall. "The plants droop because the dirt is dry," Maverick said. So he watered them every day, one can, two cans, and soon he counted four fat carrots.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Eliana went to the store with Grandma. She wanted to pick apples for a snack. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Eliana held the cart with one hand.

They walked past the bakery. Something smelled warm and sweet. Eliana saw big bread rolls on a shiny tray. She reached up her hand. "Oven," said Grandma. "Hot, hot, hot." Eliana put her hand back down. A man with a kind face touched the tray with a long silver tool. The bread went in a bag. Nobody touched the bread with bare hands.

"We count one, two, three," said Grandma. They counted apples into a bag. One, two, three red apples. Then Eliana saw something under a case. It was a small knife, shiny and sharp. "That one, I do not touch," said Eliana. Grandma nodded. A worker came and picked it up with gloves.

At the cold case, Eliana put her palm on the glass. It felt icy. "Cold glass," she said. "The bread tray is hot. The glass is cold." Grandma smiled. "That is right," she said.

At the checkout, Eliana waited for her turn. She waited and waited, slow and calm. Then the kind man from the bakery waved. "Apples for you?" he asked. Eliana held up the bag. "One, two, three," she said. She squeezed Grandma's hand, and they walked out the door together.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Emilia went to the park with Dad. It was a beautiful summer day. She stood by the gate and looked around.

"Where is the ice cream truck?" she asked.

"It came yesterday," said Dad. "Yesterday is gone. Today the truck comes later."

Emilia frowned. She wanted ice cream now. "Can we make it come now?"

"We cannot," said Dad. "But we can play first. Later comes after."

Emilia went on the swing. She slid down the slide. Then she heard a little song. Ding, ding! The truck was here!

"The truck came later!" she said. "Later comes after I play."

"Yes," said Dad. "You played, and then later came."

Emilia got a cold strawberry ice cream. She took one big lick. It dripped down her hand because the sun was hot.

"The sun makes it melt!" she said. "So I eat it now, not later."

Dad laughed. Emilia took another bite. "Tomorrow we come back," she said. "And later, the truck comes again."

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Grayson walked on the nature trail with Dad. He saw a purple flower. "Can you smell it?" asked Dad. Grayson sniffed with his nose. "My nose smells it," he said. He picked up a pine cone. His hands could feel the bumpy parts. "My hands touch it," he said.

Then a bird sang in a tree. Grayson heard the song with his ears. A butterfly landed near his shoe. He saw its wings with his eyes. Dad gave him a red apple from the bag. Grayson took a bite. "My mouth tastes it," he said. "Yum."

Then Dad held up one hand. "Tell me all five," he said. Grayson counted his fingers. "Nose, hands, ears, eyes, mouth." Dad smiled and nodded. Grayson ate the rest of the apple. "I can tell them all," he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Hannah sat on the big train seat. She was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. Hannah had her toy pig with her. She put the pig on the seat next to her. "Stay there, pig," she said.

The train went around a bend. The seat tipped a little bit. The pig slid down. Plonk! The pig fell on the floor. Hannah bent down and picked him up. She put him back on the seat. The train went around another bend. The pig slid again. Plonk! Down he went.

Hannah sat very still and thought. She looked at the pig. She looked at the bend out the window. "The train turns," said Hannah. "The pig slides because the train turns." She tried one more time. She put the pig on her lap instead. She held him with her two hands. The train turned again. The pig did not fall. He sat snug and warm.

"You stay with me now," said Hannah. The pig looked at her with his same little smile. Outside, the trees went by, green and fast. Hannah held her pig all the way.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Lydia stood in the reading corner. She wanted the bunny book. She wanted it forever.

A librarian gave her a card. It was red and little. "Your very own card," the librarian said. Lydia clapped her hands. The card said her name.

The librarian put the bunny book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "But you must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Lydia hugged the bag. "Mine forever," she whispered.

At home, Lydia read the bunny book. She read it at lunch. She read it to her teddy bear. She sang a little song about bunnies. "Hop, hop, hop," she sang.

Then Mommy said, "The book goes back tomorrow. A boy named Sam wants it next."

Lydia frowned. "I love this bunny."

"Sam loves bunnies too," said Mommy.

Lydia thought. The book made Sam happy. The book made her happy too. One bunny book, two happy kids.

The next day, Lydia walked back to the library. She gave the book to the librarian. "Here," she said. "For Sam."

Then she found a new book. A puppy book. She held it up high.

"Can I take this one home?" she asked. "And bring it back after?"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Show and Tell day was here. Weston's teacher put a big box on the floor. "Help me sort it," she said. There were three bins. One bin was for animals. One bin was for toys. One bin was for foods. Weston wanted to fill them all, but the box was very full.

Weston picked up a toy duck. "A duck is an animal," he said. He put it in the animal bin. Then the class bunny, Snowy, hopped by. Snowy nibbled the toy duck. Then Snowy hopped to the food bin and nibbled a carrot. Weston watched. "The toy duck is not food," he said. "Snowy will not eat it."

Weston picked up the toy duck again. He squeezed it. It squeaked. He did not feed it. It did not hop. "It is a toy," he said. "Snowy is the animal. Snowy eats. The duck just squeaks." He put the toy duck in the toy bin. Everyone clapped.

Then Weston heard a funny sound. He stopped to listen. Squeak, squeak! A real duck was at the window. "A duck at school!" said Weston. His teacher laughed. "That one is an animal," she said. "It can go in no bin. It will walk to the pond."
